units.translation: Middle form with accusative of the thing which one adopts: Pr. 309 μεθάρμοσαι τρόπους νέους [adapt new ways].
Let us let these things go.
the gods beneath the earth are better at taking than at letting go
having let go of my sense of shame
he let his limbs go limp
having released a drop from her heart
it is time for merchants to let down the anchor in the all-receiving houses of strangers, which I have shown should be written καθιέναι [to let down]; see under καθίημι.
we will let loose a woven lament for the city, where Hermann restored θήσομεν [we will set].
Passive Sept. 79 μεθεῖται στρατός στρατόπεδον λιπών [the army has been let go, leaving the camp], which is corrupted from καθεῖται [has been let down], about which I have spoken under καθίημι.
to stand in place of another, to withdraw, to change
I am placed in place of another, I withdraw, I change
Doric form of the aorist μετέστην

unless some ancient deity has now changed sides for the army, where several copies have στρατοῦ [of the army], which would have to be construed with δαίμων παλαιός [ancient deity]. But the dative is no less correctly placed, to be construed with the verb μεθέστηκε [has changed].

Similarly about changed fortune Sophocles fr. 572, 6: ἐν γὰρ βραχεῖ καθεῖλε κὠλίγῳ χρόνῳ πάμπλουτον ὄλβον δαίμονος κακοῦ δόσις, ὅταν μεταστῇ καὶ θεοῖς δοκῇ τάδε [for in a short time and a little while the gift of an evil deity casts down great wealth, whenever it changes and the gods so decide], where undoubtedly μεταστῆσαι [to change] should be written with L. Dindorf in the Thesaurus vol. 5 p. 671.
I have returned to the ancient track
not drinking wine made from barley
it is good to hear and to speak to later generations
the vision has gone, not later
later they honor an incurable suffering
a soothing gift of the Chryseids, those under Ilium
bringing libations to the dead as soothing offerings. Thus Casaubon for μειλίγμασι.
a soothing and charming thing of my tongue
bringing such things as are soothing to the dead
soothing this ground of the earth with rich streams

From this unused present form certain forms of the aorist and perfect are derived, about which see the Thesaurus vol. 5 p. 700-702 and Veitch p. 387. More common than the rest is the perfect passive form εἵμαρται [it has been fated] it is decreed by fate or it is fated, with the participle εἱμαρμένος [fated], of which an example in Aeschylus is Ag. 913 τὰ δ᾽ ἄλλα φροντίς θήσει δικαίως ξὺν θεοῖς εἱμαρμένα [the rest, with the gods, care will justly set as fated].
the rest, with the gods, care will justly set as fated
the gifts are less than the error
to rule over the lesser of the stronger
to be in no way less powerful than Zeus
left behind neither less nor equal
